According to video posted on social media by one Iowa farmer, an ad making the case for the Iran war, and for US support for Israel, has already started running on the Roku streaming service in the state.
Amid concerns that the Trump administration could use the power of the federal government to intimidate voters from casting ballots against Republicans, the senior federal prosecutor in south Texas released a menacing social-media video, promising to hunt down “crooked local election administrators”.
State of Israel is paying to run TV ads supporting Iran war in Iowa ahead of midterms
According to AdImpact Politics, a firm run by Donald Trump’s former campaign manager, Brad Parscale, has reserved $32,000 in advertising time to broadcast ads on behalf of the state of Israel in the Des Moines, Iowa market starting on Saturday, 24 October.
According to video posted on social media by one Iowa farmer, an ad making the case for the Iran war, and for US support for Israel, has already started running on the Roku streaming service in the state.
“I’ve been seeing these Israeli propaganda ads running for the last 2 weeks in Iowa,” the farmer wrote. “Nothing about candidates, just how Israel is good for us.”
The ad closes with a web address that directs viewers to the website Iowa4israel.com, created by Parscale’s firm, Clock Tower X, and featuring the full video.
Trump says he will not allow year-round sales of gasoline blended with 15% ethanol if Kansas elects Democratic senator
In addition to repeating a huge number of false claims about his presidency is his remarks in Kansas which have just ended, Donald Trump also frankly stated that he will only use the power of the federal government to allow year-round sales of gasoline containing higher volumes of ethanol if Kansas voters re-elect Republican senator Roger Marshall.
To make sure his message was clear, the president then said that he would block the sales if Democrat Adam Hilton wins the seat.
The year-round sale of gasoline blended with 15% ethanol has long been a priority of the biofuels industry.
Currently, gasoline containing 10% ethanol can be sold year-round, but sales of the 15% blend, known as E15, are restricted during summer months because the fuel evaporates more readily in hot weather and contributes to smog.
The Environmental Protection Agency can issue an emergency fuel waiver to allow the sale of E15 in the summer, and did so March in an attempt to lower costs for consumers amid the oil-price shock brought on by Trump’s war on Iran.
As he listed what he called the “goodies” he has granted to the people of Kansas in his remarks in Kansas on Monday, Trump said: “I also gave Kansas a waiver to sell E15 all year round. And with Roger Marshall in the Senate, we will make year round E15 permanent. But if Adam Hamilton is in, I’m not doing it. That’s it. I’m only doing it for him.”
In Kansas, Trump says he will drop tariffs on Canadian jet manufacturer key to Wichita economy
Speaking outside Wichita, Kansas on Monday, Donald Trump seemed to back off his threat to ban the sale of jets made by the Canadian manufacturer Bombardier, which employs 1,500 people in Wichita.
Last month, Trump intensified his trade war with Canada by writing on social media: “NO MORE SELLING BOMBARDIER IN THE UNITED STATES! Their products aren’t good enough!”
The announcement threatened Wichita’s economy, where the company has invested hundreds of millions of dollars and Bombardier is the third largest aerospace employer.
In his rambling remarks on Monday, the president seemed to suggest that, despite this decision he made, Kansas voters should re-elect Republican senator Roger Marshall, since he had called to try to get Trump to lift the ban on a company whose name seemed to escape him.
“Because of Roger and his phone call, I’m going to be helping a certain air company get themselves straight in a way. Is that right, Roger? I’ll be helping them,” Trump said.
“Because I always viewed them as a Canadian company. You know what I’m talking about,” the president went on, still failing to identify the company or say how, exactly, he was going to “help” them. “But now I find out they have a presence here, and we’re not hurting them if they’re in Kansas. So we’ll take care of those people.”
Trump focuses closing message on anti-Muslim racism, with attacks on Abdul El-Sayed, Ilhan Omar and Rashida Tlaib
Donald Trump made anti-Muslim racism a focus of his attacks on Democrats in remarks in Kansas on Monday, with attacks on Abdul El-Sayed, Ilhan Omar and Rashida Tlaib, and gratuitous mentions of Barack Obama’s middle name.
“Democrats are the party of Abdul Mohammad El-Sayed,” Trump said of the Michigan Senate candidate.
The president then repeated his riff about what a brilliant move it was for him to stop using El-Sayed’s first name and instead call him “Mohammed El-Sayed”, to better stoke Islamophobia.
“You know, he got very upset because I called him Mohammad. I just felt like it. Somebody said, ‘How did you do that?’ I said, ‘I’m the president, I can call him whatever the hell I want’”, Trump said.
“And actually his middle name is Mohammad,” the president added, before adding: “One good thing if you call somebody from that part of the world Mohammad, you’re about 65% sure to get it right. So if you have any problem with names, just call the guy Mohammad.”
El-Sayed responded to Trump mocking his name at a previous rally by writing on social media: “He says the name just fine when he’s begging the Qataris for a personal jet or the Saudis for funding for his son-in-law’s private equity firm.”
Despite being in Kansas to campaign for Republican senator Roger Marshall, Trump returned again and again to attacks on El-Sayed, and brought up two Muslim congresswoman, Ilhan Omar and Rashida Tlaib, who are also not from Kansas.
He also lied that both El-Sayed and his sister are members of the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist opposition group in Egypt, a wild claim that is not supported by any evidence at all but is repeated almost daily by the president.
Trump repeats wildly false claims that inflation is down and schools are performing transgender surgeries
Donald Trump’s ongoing speech to supporters in Kansas is filled with false claims he has made previously at rally after rally. Among the whoppers the president told are that inflation, which is up since he took office and started a war with Iran that has driven global oil prices sky-high, is down.
“We’ve got it cooked, the inflation,” Trump said. “Once that oil comes down, that’ll be the final straw.
Democrats, the president claimed in another wildly false tale that he tells day after day, are in favor of “transgender for everybody - the absolute mutilation of your children, where your son Timmy comes home five days later as Sarah and you don’t even know about it.”
“The worst thing they did to us is allowing 25 million people into our country totally unchecked, totally unfettered,” the president also said, wildly inflating the total number of undocumented immigrants in the United States.
Trump repeats racist false claim that rioting in France is related to immigration
Speaking in Kansas on Monday, Donald Trump repeated his entirely imaginary theory that the wave of protests and rioting in France is being led by immigrants.
In fact, as the Guardian’s Jon Henley reports from Paris, a month-long student protest by over crumbling and crowded classrooms “converged with broader frustrations over soaring living costs, rapidly widening inequality and falling public spending, bringing together students, teachers, trade unionists and a resurrected gilets jaunes movement.”
Those largely peaceful protests were hijacked by masked groups who torched vehicles, ransacked businesses and set fire to Limoges’ city hall.
Despite on-the-ground reporting on the protests from news organizations across the political spectrum, Trump and Republicans, including Fox News hosts, have insisted that the rioters in France are immigrants.
“If you want to see what is at stake in this election, just look at what’s happening in France, a once great nation that is being conquered, looted and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists and communists who hate Christianity,” Trump said, desperate to return to his obsession with nativist resentment and racism.
“They hate, frankly, the Western civilization itself,” the president went on. “And as we’re seeing in Europe, globalists, left-wing politicians have treasonously imported millions and millions of Third World migrants who are totally incompatible with West, and they are incompatible with Western values. They despise everything about France, and they’re destroying that country. And we’re not going to let that happen to this country.”
Protesters disrupt Trump rally in Kansas, where Republican fear losing US Senate seat
Protesters disrupted the first minutes of Donald Trump’s speech to a Republican midterm campaign rally in Kansas, where his party is concerned that his deeply unpopular policies could cost incumbent Republican senator Roger Marshall his seat, in the face of a strong challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton, a mega-church pastor.
Protesters quickly disrupted the event, before being led out.
US attorney in Texas threatens to hunt down 'crooked local election administrators'
Amid concerns that the Trump administration could use the power of the federal government to intimidate voters from casting ballots against Republicans in the midterm elections, the senior federal prosecutor in south Texas released a menacing social-media video on Monday, promising to hunt down “crooked local election administrators”.
The prosecutor, Aaron Reitz, is a former chief of staff to senator Ted Cruz, who was appointed US attorney for the southern district of Texas by a panel of federal judges, bypassing the usual Senate confirmation process.
Far from presenting himself as a non-partisan official, Reitz ran unsuccessfully for Texas attorney general this year, finishing fourth in the Republican primary despite promising voters he would use that office “to destroy the left”.
In the video statement released on Monday, Reitz warns that he is on the look out for “crooked local election administrators.”
“They have a duty to prevent illegal voting, and I’m here to make sure they do their job,” Reitz says. “And it means no fraud, accurate voter roles, honest paperwork, secure ballots, and lawful procedures are essential to a fraud-free election.”
“So, let me be clear: if you violate federal election law, I will hunt you down and prosecute you,” Reitz warns.
“Election day is Tuesday, November 3rd,” he concludes. “We’ll see you out at the polls.”
Our colleague David Smith reports from Park City, Kansas, where Donald Trump is scheduled to address a Republican campaign rally, that the president’s false claim that rioting in France is driven by immigrants preceded him.
Donald Trump’s latest campaign rally has kicked off with something unusual: riots in France.
With supporters still filing into a 5,000-seat multi-purpose arena in Park City, Kansas, giant TV screens played about 10 minutes’ of Fox News coverage of the unrest that has gripped Paris and other cities. It included commentary blaming the trouble on the French government’s immigration policies.
That matches current Republican talking points, which seized on the unruly protests to demonise multiculturalism and defend “America first” nationalism ahead of the midterm elections.
As he set off for Kansas, Trump told reporters at the White House that he had warned French president Emmanuel Macron he was “making a big mistake”. Trump said: “The whole world was coming in, and as you know, Paris is going to be a Muslim city very soon, and that wasn’t the deal … We closed our borders. He didn’t.”
The official White House X account posted on Monday. “If you import the third world, you become the third world.” Vice-president JD Vance and an array of Republican politicians have lined up to make the same argument.
House Speaker Mike Johnson posted: “France is descending into chaos because they wanted OPEN BORDERS – just like the socialist Democrats in America. What we are witnessing is a chilling warning for all Americans of what happens if the radical Marxist insurgent left gets their way.” Senator Eric Schmitt added: “The anti-civilization Left is devouring France. It will devour America if we let it.”
Trump is in Kansas to rally for Republican Roger Marshall, facing a surprisingly tough challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton, who has outraised him by a big margin. No Democrat has won a US Senate seat in Kansas since 1932.
A month-long protest by high school pupils over crumbling and crowded classrooms converged with broader frustrations over soaring living costs, rapidly widening inequality and falling public spending, bringing together students, teachers, trade unionists and a resurrected gilets jaunes movement.
Those largely peaceful protests were swiftly hijacked by masked groups who torched vehicles, ransacked businesses and severely damaged public infrastructure, including setting fire to Limoges’ city hall and invading that of Marseille.
Trump's claim 'a million' Ukrainians have been killed contradicted by evidence
Before we move on from Donald Trump’s latest attempt to blame Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, for the death of “a million” Ukrainians since the full-scale Russian invasion in 2022, it is worth pausing for a moment to explain that this number, which Trump has been repeating for two years, is false.
While the exact death toll is not known, a study published in July by the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington, estimated that “Ukrainian forces have suffered somewhere between 525,000 and 625,000 casualties (killed, wounded, and missing) and between 125,000 and 150,000 fatalities between February 2022 and June 2026.”
The same study concluded that the Russian military “has suffered 1.4 million battlefield casualties and as many as 450,000 deaths since its February 2022 full-scale invasion”.
Despite the evidence, Trump has been wildly inflating the Ukrainian death toll in public comments for two years. On the campaign trail in October 2024, Trump claimed that there were “millions of dead people” as a result of the war in Ukraine at that time.
Four months later, after he returned to the Oval Office, Trump told a national prayer breakfast in Washington that there were “probably 800,000 Russians; 600,000 – 700,000 Ukrainians, young people, just laying on a battlefield dead”.
Two months after that, when Trump was asked to comment on Russia’s Palm Sunday attack on Ukraine, Trump said “This country would’ve never allowed that war to have started if I were president. That war is a shame. Millions of people are dead”.
Last week, Trump attacked Zelenskyy for resisting the Russian invasion, saying: “You’ve lost 30% of your country and you’ve had over a million people killed.”
In August of this year, the United Nations reported that more civilians were killed or injured in Ukraine in July than in any month since March 2022.
Overall, since 24 February 2022, the UN said it has verified that at least 16,874 civilians killed have been killed in Ukraine, including 820 children, and 51,273 injured, including 3,126 children.”
Vance speech disrupted by protester shouting 'release the Epstein files'; he replies with a racist joke
A protester disrupted a speech by JD Vance, the US vice-president, in North Carolina on Monday, shouting “Release the Epstein files! God bless our children!” before being led away.
The protester, who was positioned directly behind Vance during a midterm campaign rally in support of Republican candidates, was seen on a live video stream standing up and shouting about 10 minutes into the vice-president’s speech.
As the man was led away the crowd booed the interruption, and chanted “U!S!A!”
Vance then attempted to joke that the man, a person of color who spoke with an American accent, must be an undocumented immigrant.
“Ladies and gentlemen, I’m going to have to amend something I said earlier. I said that we have had zero illegal border crossings in the United States of America,” Vance said to laughter from the crowd. “But one isn’t bad, right?”
New Reuters poll shows Trump's approval rating dropping to a record low
A new poll by Reuters shows that only 31% of Americans approve of Donald Trump’s performance in office, a percentage point lower than the survey from two weeks ago and a record low for the president.
It comes as Trump embarks on another campaign sprint to help beleaguered Republicans in competitive midterm races.
When asked which party they would vote for if the elections were held today, 47% of registered voters in the nationwide poll picked Democrats, while 35% chose Republicans.
'It's time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine': Trump slams Zelenskyy and defends lifting Russian sanctions
Trump again rebuked the idea that his move to waive sanctions for Russia last week was ultimately to hand Moscow a win.
“I’m supporting stopping the war between Russia and Ukraine,” Trump told reporters. “Frankly, Zelenskyy is not helping matters much. I think he doesn’t want to stop it, but I want to see people not die.”
In response to Zelenskyy saying that the US president is on the “wrong side of history”, Trump snapped back.
“If he would have listened to me, he would have made a much better deal a long time ago, and he’d have a million people living from his side,” Trump said. “I think it’s time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine …. Very little land has moved, but a million people, a tremendous number of people, are dead.”
Ahead of leaving for a campaign rally in Wichita, Kansas, Donald Trump again claimed – without evidence – that the riots throughout France were due to mass migration.
“I told Emmanuel [Macron], you should close up your borders,” the US president said. “I’ve known him for probably eight or nine years. I told him as soon as I met him, I said, ‘you’re making a big mistake’. We closed our borders. He didn’t.”
Attorneys for Mahmoud Khalil, the former Columbia University student who has become the symbol of the Trump administration’s crusade against pro-Palestinian speech, have petitioned the US supreme court to review his case – the final chapter in a months-long legal saga that could determine countless foreign citizens’ ability to challenge their detention by US immigration authorities in federal court.
Khalil, a US permanent resident who was born in a Palestinian refugee camp in Syria, was arrested in his Columbia housing in March 2025, the first of several foreign students and scholars the Trump administration targeted over their advocacy for Palestinian rights. He was detained for more than three months in an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facility in Louisiana before a federal judge in New Jersey, where he had been briefly held before ICE moved him, ordered him released while his immigration process proceeds.
“This fight is not only about whether I get to stay in this country, it’s really about whether anyone in this country can speak out for Palestinians without being punished for it,” Khalil said during a press conference on Monday.
The US departments of state, justice and homeland security did not respond to requests for comment.
The government has cited an obscure McCarthy-era law to argue that Khalil and the other scholars’ pro-Palestinian expression posed a threat to US foreign policy objectives.
So far, no court has fully weighed in on the constitutionality of the law, with legal arguments instead focused on whether district courts have the authority to order people released from immigration detention while their immigration cases are under way. Khalil’s attorneys and immigrants rights advocates warn that if the supreme court rules the district courts lack such authority, that would effectively result in people the government has detained unconstitutionally to languish in immigration detention with no recourse, potentially for months or years.
The justice department announced the arrest of 28 legal permanent residents in California “who are charged in criminal complaints with federal crimes, including that they fraudulently registered to vote in US elections, electoral contests in which most of them cast illegal and fraudulently obtained ballots”. Non-citizen voting is extremely rare, andthe 28 who have allegedly committed crimes, would be an exceptionally small fraction of the 174 million people who were registered to vote in the 2024 presidential election.The arrests come just days after the administration sued the Golden state, to prevent it from counting mail-in ballots from people the federal government has allegedly identified as “likely” noncitizens.
New polling also shows that a majority (66%) of Americans believe Trump is using the presidency to enrich himself. Looking at that data from the Washington Post and ABC even further, 34% of Republicans believe Trump is enriching himself – a 12-point jump from last September. More here
Meanwhile, Trump heads to Kansas today to kick off a seven-state campaign blitz this week in parts of the country he carried in 2024, as unexpectedly tight races in GOP strongholds stoke fears of sweeping Democratic gains in next month’s midterms. With 15 days until the 3 November vote, Trump’s rally on the outskirts of Wichita aims to shore up the incumbent Republican senator Roger Marshall, who is locked in a dead heat with his Democratic opponent Adam Hamilton. He’ll follow up with rallies in the Carolinas, Iowa, Florida, Georgia and Michigan over the next six days.
More US representatives reported todaythat their offices had been sent suspicious letters, after the FBI and the US Postal Inspection Service said they were investigating letters sent to state officials and election offices across the country containing an “unknown substance” last week. On Monday, congressman Suhas Subramanyam, a Virginia Democrat, said his office in Leesburg received an envelope “containing a suspicious substance” and staff were “promptly evacuated”. Similarly, in Maine, Democratic representative Chellie Pingree said that her office also received “a suspicious letter consistent with those received by many other congressional and election offices in recent days”.
In a bipartisan call with GOP Senator Thom Tillis and Senator Richard Blumenthal, a Democrat, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Ukraine’s access to Starlink satellite services “remain degraded” and “disruptions to US intelligence sharing” persist, when it comes to the “early warning of Russian ballistic missile launches”. Last week, the two lawmakers called on the Pentagon’s inspector general to investigate Ukraine’s disruptions accessing Starshield – the military version of Starlink’s satellite network built for governments and defense agencies – and in a statement today they said that Zelenskyy reiterated his “willingness to halt strikes on Russian energy facilities as President Trump has proposed, but only if [Vladimir] Putin agrees to the same”.
A man who heckled the Democratic candidate for Senate Abdul El-Sayed and demanded he disavow the Muslim Brotherhood at a Michigan town hall is a former aide to the Republican senator Josh Hawley, according to congressional staff records.
At the event on Saturday, an attender who gave his name only as “Tommy” shouted from the crowd, asking whether El-Sayed would disavow the movement. El-Sayed answered: “Sure, yeah, absolutely,” then turned the question around, asking whether the man assumed he wouldn’t.
Tommy said he had simply not heard El-Sayed reject the Muslim Brotherhood, one of the Arab world’s oldest and most influential Islamist movements. Under Trump the US has moved to designate certain chapters of the group as foreign terrorist organizations.
Over nearly five minutes at the town hall, El-Sayed pointed to how the question shouted by Tommy carried an implication of “dual loyalty”, comparing it with the doubts once raised about John F Kennedy’s Catholicism, and told the room he was running for the Senate and “happen[s] to be Muslim”.
He then asked Tommy whether he would disavow any attempt to read religious doctrine into American law. Tommy said he would not. El-Sayed answered that it was Tommy who needed to understand the constitution, drawing cheers, and the man left the room.
The questioner has since been identified as Thomas Teepell, whose staff records show he joined Hawley’s office as an intern in 2023 and rose to operations director before leaving in February. He then became political director for Philip Sarnecki’s Kansas gubernatorial campaign. Sarnecki lost the Republican primary on 4 August.
Teepell is the son of the Republican strategist Timmy Teepell, a longtime adviser to Hawley and the former Louisiana governor Bobby Jindal. The Handbasket first reported the identification.
The question echoes a line of attack that Republicans have tried to push against El-Sayed for weeks, including when Rogers raised alleged Brotherhood ties during one of their debates.
Zelenskyy tells lawmakers that Starlink services 'remain degraded'; US intelligence sharing disruptions persist
In a bipartisan call with GOP Senator Thom Tillis and Senator Richard Blumenthal, a Democrat, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Ukraine’s access to Starlink satellite services “remain degraded” and “disruptions to US intelligence sharing” persist, when it comes to the “early warning of Russian ballistic missile launches”.
Last week, the two lawmakers called on the Pentagon’s inspector general to investigate Ukraine’s disruptions accessing Starshield – the military version of Starlink’s satellite network built for governments and defense agencies – and in a statement today they said that Zelenskyy reiterated his “willingness to halt strikes on Russian energy facilities as President Trump has proposed, but only if [Vladimir] Putin agrees to the same”.
Zelenskyy’s call with Washington lawmakers comes after he said that Ukraine did not receive a warning from the US about an impending Russian missile attack on Sunday evening, as my colleague Andrew Roth reports from Kyiv. On Friday, Trump waived a sweeping package of sanctions on Russia – a move he claimed was to prevent driving Russia “away from the bargaining table”.

Trump says he will not allow year-round sales of gasoline blended with 15% ethanol if Kansas elects Democratic senator

To make sure his message was clear, the president then said that he would block the sales if Democrat Adam Hilton wins the seat.
The year-round sale of gasoline blended with 15% ethanol has long been a priority of the biofuels industry.

The Environmental Protection Agency can issue an emergency fuel waiver to allow the sale of E15 in the summer, and did so March in an attempt to lower costs for consumers amid the oil-price shock brought on by Trump’s war on Iran.
As he listed what he called the “goodies” he has granted to the people of Kansas in his remarks in Kansas on Monday, Trump said: “I also gave Kansas a waiver to sell E15 all year round. In the video statement released on Monday, Reitz warns that he is on the look out for “crooked local election administrators.”
“They have a duty to prevent illegal voting, and I’m here to make sure they do their job,” Reitz says. “And it means no fraud, accurate voter roles, honest paperwork, secure ballots, and lawful procedures are essential to a fraud-free election.”
“So, let me be clear: if you violate federal election law, I will hunt you down and prosecute you,” Reitz warns.
“Election day is Tuesday, November 3rd,” he concludes. “We’ll see you out at the polls.”
Our colleague David Smith reports from Park City, Kansas, where Donald Trump is scheduled to address a Republican campaign rally, that the president’s false claim that rioting in France is driven by immigrants preceded him.
Donald Trump’s latest campaign rally has kicked off with something unusual: riots in France.
With supporters still filing into a 5,000-seat multi-purpose arena in Park City, Kansas, giant TV screens played about 10 minutes’ of Fox News coverage of the unrest that has gripped Paris and other cities. It included commentary blaming the trouble on the French government’s immigration policies.
That matches current Republican talking points, which seized on the unruly protests to demonise multiculturalism and defend “America first” nationalism ahead of the midterm elections.
As he set off for Kansas, Trump told reporters at the White House that he had warned French president Emmanuel Macron he was “making a big mistake”. Trump said: “The whole world was coming in, and as you know, Paris is going to be a Muslim city very soon, and that wasn’t the deal … We closed our borders. He didn’t.”
The official White House X account posted on Monday. “If you import the third world, you become the third world.” Vice-president JD Vance and an array of Republican politicians have lined up to make the same argument.
House Speaker Mike Johnson posted: “France is descending into chaos because they wanted OPEN BORDERS – just like the socialist Democrats in America. What we are witnessing is a chilling warning for all Americans of what happens if the radical Marxist insurgent left gets their way.” Senator Eric Schmitt added: “The anti-civilization Left is devouring France. It will devour America if we let it.”
Trump is in Kansas to rally for Republican Roger Marshall, facing a surprisingly tough challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton, who has outraised him by a big margin. No Democrat has won a US Senate seat in Kansas since 1932.
A month-long protest by high school pupils over crumbling and crowded classrooms converged with broader frustrations over soaring living costs, rapidly widening inequality and falling public spending, bringing together students, teachers, trade unionists and a resurrected gilets jaunes movement.
Those largely peaceful protests were swiftly hijacked by masked groups who torched vehicles, ransacked businesses and severely damaged public infrastructure, including setting fire to Limoges’ city hall and invading that of Marseille.
Trump's claim 'a million' Ukrainians have been killed contradicted by evidence
Before we move on from Donald Trump’s latest attempt to blame Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, for the death of “a million” Ukrainians since the full-scale Russian invasion in 2022, it is worth pausing for a moment to explain that this number, which Trump has been repeating for two years, is false.
While the exact death toll is not known, a study published in July by the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington, estimated that “Ukrainian forces have suffered somewhere between 525,000 and 625,000 casualties (killed, wounded, and missing) and between 125,000 and 150,000 fatalities between February 2022 and June 2026.”
The same study concluded that the Russian military “has suffered 1.4 million battlefield casualties and as many as 450,000 deaths since its February 2022 full-scale invasion”.
Despite the evidence, Trump has been wildly inflating the Ukrainian death toll in public comments for two years. On the campaign trail in October 2024, Trump claimed that there were “millions of dead people” as a result of the war in Ukraine at that time.
Four months later, after he returned to the Oval Office, Trump told a national prayer breakfast in Washington that there were “probably 800,000 Russians; 600,000 – 700,000 Ukrainians, young people, just laying on a battlefield dead”.
Two months after that, when Trump was asked to comment on Russia’s Palm Sunday attack on Ukraine, Trump said “This country would’ve never allowed that war to have started if I were president. That war is a shame. Millions of people are dead”.
Last week, Trump attacked Zelenskyy for resisting the Russian invasion, saying: “You’ve lost 30% of your country and you’ve had over a million people killed.”
In August of this year, the United Nations reported that more civilians were killed or injured in Ukraine in July than in any month since March 2022.
Overall, since 24 February 2022, the UN said it has verified that at least 16,874 civilians killed have been killed in Ukraine, including 820 children, and 51,273 injured, including 3,126 children.”
Vance speech disrupted by protester shouting 'release the Epstein files'; he replies with a racist joke
A protester disrupted a speech by JD Vance, the US vice-president, in North Carolina on Monday, shouting “Release the Epstein files! God bless our children!” before being led away.
The protester, who was positioned directly behind Vance during a midterm campaign rally in support of Republican candidates, was seen on a live video stream standing up and shouting about 10 minutes into the vice-president’s speech.
As the man was led away the crowd booed the interruption, and chanted “U!S!A!”
Vance then attempted to joke that the man, a person of color who spoke with an American accent, must be an undocumented immigrant.
“Ladies and gentlemen, I’m going to have to amend something I said earlier. I said that we have had zero illegal border crossings in the United States of America,” Vance said to laughter from the crowd. “But one isn’t bad, right?”
New Reuters poll shows Trump's approval rating dropping to a record low
A new poll by Reuters shows that only 31% of Americans approve of Donald Trump’s performance in office, a percentage point lower than the survey from two weeks ago and a record low for the president.
It comes as Trump embarks on another campaign sprint to help beleaguered Republicans in competitive midterm races.
When asked which party they would vote for if the elections were held today, 47% of registered voters in the nationwide poll picked Democrats, while 35% chose Republicans.
'It's time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine': Trump slams Zelenskyy and defends lifting Russian sanctions
Trump again rebuked the idea that his move to waive sanctions for Russia last week was ultimately to hand Moscow a win.
“I’m supporting stopping the war between Russia and Ukraine,” Trump told reporters. “Frankly, Zelenskyy is not helping matters much. I think he doesn’t want to stop it, but I want to see people not die.”
In response to Zelenskyy saying that the US president is on the “wrong side of history”, Trump snapped back.
“If he would have listened to me, he would have made a much better deal a long time ago, and he’d have a million people living from his side,” Trump said. “I think it’s time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine …. Very little land has moved, but a million people, a tremendous number of people, are dead.”
Ahead of leaving for a campaign rally in Wichita, Kansas, Donald Trump again claimed – without evidence – that the riots throughout France were due to mass migration.
“I told Emmanuel [Macron], you should close up your borders,” the US president said. “I’ve known him for probably eight or nine years. I told him as soon as I met him, I said, ‘you’re making a big mistake’. We closed our borders. He didn’t.”
Attorneys for Mahmoud Khalil, the former Columbia University student who has become the symbol of the Trump administration’s crusade against pro-Palestinian speech, have petitioned the US supreme court to review his case – the final chapter in a months-long legal saga that could determine countless foreign citizens’ ability to challenge their detention by US immigration authorities in federal court.
Khalil, a US permanent resident who was born in a Palestinian refugee camp in Syria, was arrested in his Columbia housing in March 2025, the first of several foreign students and scholars the Trump administration targeted over their advocacy for Palestinian rights. He was detained for more than three months in an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facility in Louisiana before a federal judge in New Jersey, where he had been briefly held before ICE moved him, ordered him released while his immigration process proceeds.
“This fight is not only about whether I get to stay in this country, it’s really about whether anyone in this country can speak out for Palestinians without being punished for it,” Khalil said during a press conference on Monday.
The US departments of state, justice and homeland security did not respond to requests for comment.
The government has cited an obscure McCarthy-era law to argue that Khalil and the other scholars’ pro-Palestinian expression posed a threat to US foreign policy objectives.
So far, no court has fully weighed in on the constitutionality of the law, with legal arguments instead focused on whether district courts have the authority to order people released from immigration detention while their immigration cases are under way. Khalil’s attorneys and immigrants rights advocates warn that if the supreme court rules the district courts lack such authority, that would effectively result in people the government has detained unconstitutionally to languish in immigration detention with no recourse, potentially for months or years.
The justice department announced the arrest of 28 legal permanent residents in California “who are charged in criminal complaints with federal crimes, including that they fraudulently registered to vote in US elections, electoral contests in which most of them cast illegal and fraudulently obtained ballots”. Non-citizen voting is extremely rare, andthe 28 who have allegedly committed crimes, would be an exceptionally small fraction of the 174 million people who were registered to vote in the 2024 presidential election.The arrests come just days after the administration sued the Golden state, to prevent it from counting mail-in ballots from people the federal government has allegedly identified as “likely” noncitizens.
New polling also shows that a majority (66%) of Americans believe Trump is using the presidency to enrich himself. Looking at that data from the Washington Post and ABC even further, 34% of Republicans believe Trump is enriching himself – a 12-point jump from last September. More here
Meanwhile, Trump heads to Kansas today to kick off a seven-state campaign blitz this week in parts of the country he carried in 2024, as unexpectedly tight races in GOP strongholds stoke fears of sweeping Democratic gains in next month’s midterms. With 15 days until the 3 November vote, Trump’s rally on the outskirts of Wichita aims to shore up the incumbent Republican senator Roger Marshall, who is locked in a dead heat with his Democratic opponent Adam Hamilton. He’ll follow up with rallies in the Carolinas, Iowa, Florida, Georgia and Michigan over the next six days.
More US representatives reported todaythat their offices had been sent suspicious letters, after the FBI and the US Postal Inspection Service said they were investigating letters sent to state officials and election offices across the country containing an “unknown substance” last week. On Monday, congressman Suhas Subramanyam, a Virginia Democrat, said his office in Leesburg received an envelope “containing a suspicious substance” and staff were “promptly evacuated”. Similarly, in Maine, Democratic representative Chellie Pingree said that her office also received “a suspicious letter consistent with those received by many other congressional and election offices in recent days”.
In a bipartisan call with GOP Senator Thom Tillis and Senator Richard Blumenthal, a Democrat, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Ukraine’s access to Starlink satellite services “remain degraded” and “disruptions to US intelligence sharing” persist, when it comes to the “early warning of Russian ballistic missile launches”. Last week, the two lawmakers called on the Pentagon’s inspector general to investigate Ukraine’s disruptions accessing Starshield – the military version of Starlink’s satellite network built for governments and defense agencies – and in a statement today they said that Zelenskyy reiterated his “willingness to halt strikes on Russian energy facilities as President Trump has proposed, but only if [Vladimir] Putin agrees to the same”.
A man who heckled the Democratic candidate for Senate Abdul El-Sayed and demanded he disavow the Muslim Brotherhood at a Michigan town hall is a former aide to the Republican senator Josh Hawley, according to congressional staff records.
At the event on Saturday, an attender who gave his name only as “Tommy” shouted from the crowd, asking whether El-Sayed would disavow the movement. El-Sayed answered: “Sure, yeah, absolutely,” then turned the question around, asking whether the man assumed he wouldn’t.
Tommy said he had simply not heard El-Sayed reject the Muslim Brotherhood, one of the Arab world’s oldest and most influential Islamist movements. Under Trump the US has moved to designate certain chapters of the group as foreign terrorist organizations.
Over nearly five minutes at the town hall, El-Sayed pointed to how the question shouted by Tommy carried an implication of “dual loyalty”, comparing it with the doubts once raised about John F Kennedy’s Catholicism, and told the room he was running for the Senate and “happen[s] to be Muslim”.
He then asked Tommy whether he would disavow any attempt to read religious doctrine into American law. Tommy said he would not. El-Sayed answered that it was Tommy who needed to understand the constitution, drawing cheers, and the man left the room.
The questioner has since been identified as Thomas Teepell, whose staff records show he joined Hawley’s office as an intern in 2023 and rose to operations director before leaving in February. He then became political director for Philip Sarnecki’s Kansas gubernatorial campaign. Sarnecki lost the Republican primary on 4 August.
Teepell is the son of the Republican strategist Timmy Teepell, a longtime adviser to Hawley and the former Louisiana governor Bobby Jindal. The Handbasket first reported the identification.
The question echoes a line of attack that Republicans have tried to push against El-Sayed for weeks, including when Rogers raised alleged Brotherhood ties during one of their debates.
Zelenskyy tells lawmakers that Starlink services 'remain degraded'; US intelligence sharing disruptions persist
In a bipartisan call with GOP Senator Thom Tillis and Senator Richard Blumenthal, a Democrat, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Ukraine’s access to Starlink satellite services “remain degraded” and “disruptions to US intelligence sharing” persist, when it comes to the “early warning of Russian ballistic missile launches”.
Last week, the two lawmakers called on the Pentagon’s inspector general to investigate Ukraine’s disruptions accessing Starshield – the military version of Starlink’s satellite network built for governments and defense agencies – and in a statement today they said that Zelenskyy reiterated his “willingness to halt strikes on Russian energy facilities as President Trump has proposed, but only if [Vladimir] Putin agrees to the same”.
Zelenskyy’s call with Washington lawmakers comes after he said that Ukraine did not receive a warning from the US about an impending Russian missile attack on Sunday evening, as my colleague Andrew Roth reports from Kyiv. On Friday, Trump waived a sweeping package of sanctions on Russia – a move he claimed was to prevent driving Russia “away from the bargaining table”.

title: Kritik an Rot-Grün-Rot in Berlin: "Ich habe noch erhebliche Zweifel"
content_c:
Rot-Grün-Rot in Berlin geplant "Ich habe noch erhebliche Zweifel"
Die rot-grün-roten Sondierungsgespräche in Berlin waren holprig, aber erfolgreich. Heute wollen Grüne und SPD über Koalitionsverhandlungen mit der Linken entscheiden. Doch Kritik und Zweifel sind laut, etwa bei SPD-Fraktionschef Miersch.
Nach den erfolgreichen Sondierungsgesprächen wollen SPD und Grüne in Berlin heute über die Aufnahme von Koalitionsverhandlungen mit der Linken entscheiden. Die Grünen haben dazu einen kleinen Parteitag am Abend einberufen. Die SPD berät digital darüber. Die Linke will am 31. Oktober entscheiden.
Miersch hat "erhebliche Zweifel"
Doch in der schwarz-roten Koalition wächst die Kritik an einem möglichen Regierungsbündnis unter Führung der Linkspartei in der Hauptstadt.
"Ich habe noch erhebliche Zweifel", sagte der Chef der SPD-Bundestagsfraktion, Matthias Miersch, in der ARD-Sendung "Caren Miosga". Vor allem Teile der Berliner Linken hätten aus seiner Sicht Fragen zum Umgang mit Antisemitismus und Clan-Kriminalität nicht ausreichend geklärt. Die SPD trage eine große Verantwortung und müsse sich genau überlegen, mit wem sie zusammenarbeite.
Erklärung von SPD-Abgeordneten
Miersch bestätigte zugleich, dass sich 20 SPD-Bundestagsabgeordnete kritisch geäußert hätten. So kursiert eine Erklärung, in dem sich Mitglieder der SPD-Fraktion gegen eine Koalition mit der Linken in Berlin wenden. "Unser Wertekompass ist niemals verhandelbar", lautet die Überschrift des Papiers. Darüber berichteten etwa der Spiegel, die Bild und Table.Briefings, denen nach eigenen Angaben jeweils das Papier vorlag.
Die wiederkehrenden Antisemitismuskonflikte im Berliner Landesverband der Linken, die Kontakte in das Remmo-Umfeld, also zu einem kriminellen Clan, sowie zu Akteuren aus extremistischen Milieus und der Umgang mit diesen Vorgängen begründeten "einen erheblichen Zweifel" an der politischen Verlässlichkeit des Landesverbandes, zitierten die Medien aus der Erklärung.
Man respektiere die Entscheidungshoheit der Berliner SPD. "Als Mitglieder der SPD-Bundestagsfraktion sehen wir zugleich unsere Verantwortung für die Glaubwürdigkeit gemeinsamer sozialdemokratischer Grundsätze. Deshalb sprechen wir uns unter den gegenwärtigen Voraussetzungen mit Nachdruck gegen die Aufnahme von Koalitionsverhandlungen mit der Berliner Linken aus", heißt es laut den Medienberichten in der Erklärung.
Heil zweifelt an Regierungsfähigkeit
Auch der frühere Arbeitsminister Hubertus Heil, der als ein möglicher Kandidat für den SPD-Chefposten gehandelt wird, äußerte Skepsis. Angesichts "der Art und Weise, wie sich die Linkspartei hier in Berlin benimmt, sind Zweifel an der Regierungsfähigkeit angebracht", sagte der SPD-Politiker im Bericht aus Berlin. Die Linkspartei in Berlin unterscheide sich deutlich von der in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, wo ebenfalls gerade eine Koalition von SPD, Grünen und Linken gebildet werden soll.
Grünen-Chefin verweist auf Erklärung
Die Grünen-Vorsitzende Franziska Brantner verwies im Bericht aus Berlin auf die Erklärung der drei Parteien, in der Antisemitismus und Clan-Verbindungen ausgeschlossen werden. Sie betonte, sie erwarte, dass die Ankündigungen konsequent umgesetzt würden. "Ansonsten wird es keine stabile Regierung werden können", sagte sie.
Ähnlich äußerte sich Fraktionschefin Katharina Dröge. Es sei unerlässlich, dass Die Linke Antisemitismus-Beschlüsse auch in die Praxis umsetze, sagte sie im Deutschlandfunk.
Eine gemeinsame Erklärung zum Thema Antisemitismus soll in einen möglichen gemeinsamen Koalitionsvertrag aufgenommen werden.
Unmut über Pläne für Vergesellschaftung
Kritik an einem rot-grün-roten Bündnis gibt es nicht nur wegen des Umgangs mit Antisemitismus. Auch die Pläne für eine Vergesellschaftung großer Wohnungskonzerne sorgt für Unmut. In dem am Samstag vorgelegten Sondierungspapier von Linken, Grünen und SPD ist die Rede davon, Immobilienkonzerne mit mehr als 10.000 Wohnungen zu vergesellschaften. Dafür sollen bis zu 16 Milliarden Euro als Entschädigungssumme bereit gestellt werden.
Miersch sagte, um die Pläne umzusetzen müssten "wahnsinnige Entschädigungssummen" fließen, die man besser in den Wohnungsbau stecken sollte. Vergesellschaftung sei der falsche Weg.
Jusos für Koalitionsgespräche
Ein klares Ja für eine Koalition mit Grünen und Linken in Berlin kommt von Juso-Chef Philipp Türmer. Der Vorsitzende der SPD-Jugendorganisation sagte im ARD-Morgenmagazin, er sehe eine Chance in einem rot-grün-roten Bündnis. Vor allem die Krise auf dem Wohnungsmarkt könnte gemildert werden.
"Die Berlinerinnen und Berliner haben klargemacht, dass sie sich einen Politikwechsel wünschen", insbesondere bei den hohen Mieten, so Türmer. "Sie vertrauen diesem Bündnis, dass sie endlich etwas dagegen machen."
Ein Gesetz gegen Vergesellschaftung hält Türmer für unrealistisch. "Ich halte es für verfassungswidrig, den Ländern etwas zu verbieten, was die Verfassung ihnen garantiert."
Scharfe Kritik von CDU und CSU
Aus der Union kommt besonders scharfe Kritik an den Plänen für Vergesellschaftung. CSU-Chef Markus Söder sprach beim "Deutschlandtag" der Jungen Union von absurden Enteignungsfantasien von Sozialisten.
Unionsfraktionschef Thorsten Frei bezeichnete Vergesellschaftungen als das Dümmste, was man machen könne. Es werde Geld, das Berlin nicht habe, für Wohnungen ausgegeben, die es schon gebe. Zudem würden Investoren verschreckt, so Frei bei Caren Miosga.
Pläne für Verbot von Vergesellschaftungen
Die Bundesregierung hatte bereits im Juli beschlossen, dass sie eine solche Überführung in Gemeineigentum, die das Grundgesetz prinzipiell erlaubt, verhindern will. Vor allem die Union befürchtet durch die rot-grün-roten Pläne einen Schaden für den Wirtschaftsstandort Deutschland.
Bislang gibt es allerdings noch keinen Gesetzentwurf, sondern nur einen Beschluss des Koalitionsausschusses.
Bei einer Enteignung nach Artikel 14 des Grundgesetzes (GG) werden konkrete Eigentumsrechte für bestimmte Vorhaben, die dem "Wohle der Allgemeinheit" dienen, entzogen - etwa Grundstücke für eine Autobahn oder einen Deich. Wollen die Grundstückseigentümer nicht verkaufen, können sie in bestimmten Fällen enteignet werden. Dafür gibt es eingespielte rechtliche Verfahren mit Entschädigungszahlungen für die enteigneten Besitzer. Allein im Straßenbau gibt es jedes Jahr eine dreistellige Zahl an Enteignungsverfahren.
Bei einer Vergesellschaftung nach Artikel 15 GG geht es hingegen darum, "Grund und Boden, Naturschätze und Produktionsmittel" in Gemeineigentum zu überführen. Allerdings kam Artikel 15 noch nie zur Anwendung. Es geht damit um absolutes rechtliches Neuland. Auch hier müssten Art und Ausmaß der Entschädigung gesetzlich geregelt werden. Die Bezeichnung Enteignung ist in der politischen Debatte verständlich, juristisch aber unpräzise.

Darüber berichteten etwa der Spiegel, die Bild und Table.Briefings, denen nach eigenen Angaben jeweils das Papier vorlag.
Die wiederkehrenden Antisemitismuskonflikte im Berliner Landesverband der Linken, die Kontakte in das Remmo-Umfeld, also zu einem kriminellen Clan, sowie zu Akteuren aus extremistischen Milieus und der Umgang mit diesen Vorgängen begründeten "einen erheblichen Zweifel" an der politischen Verlässlichkeit des Landesverbandes, zitierten die Medien aus der Erklärung.
Man respektiere die Entscheidungshoheit der Berliner SPD. "Als Mitglieder der SPD-Bundestagsfraktion sehen wir zugleich unsere Verantwortung für die Glaubwürdigkeit gemeinsamer sozialdemokratischer Grundsätze. Deshalb sprechen wir uns unter den gegenwärtigen Voraussetzungen mit Nachdruck gegen die Aufnahme von Koalitionsverhandlungen mit der Berliner Linken aus", heißt es laut den Medienberichten in der Erklärung.
Heil zweifelt an Regierungsfähigkeit
Auch der frühere Arbeitsminister Hubertus Heil, der als ein möglicher Kandidat für den SPD-Chefposten gehandelt wird, äußerte Skepsis. Angesichts "der Art und Weise, wie sich die Linkspartei hier in Berlin benimmt, sind Zweifel an der Regierungsfähigkeit angebracht", sagte der SPD-Politiker im Bericht aus Berlin. Die Linkspartei in Berlin unterscheide sich deutlich von der in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, wo ebenfalls gerade eine Koalition von SPD, Grünen und Linken gebildet werden soll.
Grünen-Chefin verweist auf Erklärung
Die Grünen-Vorsitzende Franziska Brantner verwies im Bericht aus Berlin auf die Erklärung der drei Parteien, in der Antisemitismus und Clan-Verbindungen ausgeschlossen werden. Sie betonte, sie erwarte, dass die Ankündigungen konsequent umgesetzt würden. "Ansonsten wird es keine stabile Regierung werden können", sagte sie.
Ähnlich äußerte sich Fraktionschefin Katharina Dröge. Es sei unerlässlich, dass Die Linke Antisemitismus-Beschlüsse auch in die Praxis umsetze, sagte sie im Deutschlandfunk.
Eine gemeinsame Erklärung zum Thema Antisemitismus soll in einen möglichen gemeinsamen Koalitionsvertrag aufgenommen werden.
Unmut über Pläne für Vergesellschaftung
Kritik an einem rot-grün-roten Bündnis gibt es nicht nur wegen des Umgangs mit Antisemitismus. Auch die Pläne für eine Vergesellschaftung großer Wohnungskonzerne sorgt für Unmut. In dem am Samstag vorgelegten Sondierungspapier von Linken, Grünen und SPD ist die Rede davon, Immobilienkonzerne mit mehr als 10.000 Wohnungen zu vergesellschaften. Dafür sollen bis zu 16 Milliarden Euro als Entschädigungssumme bereit gestellt werden.
Miersch sagte, um die Pläne umzusetzen müssten "wahnsinnige Entschädigungssummen" fließen, die man besser in den Wohnungsbau stecken sollte. Vergesellschaftung sei der falsche Weg.
Jusos für Koalitionsgespräche
Ein klares Ja für eine Koalition mit Grünen und Linken in Berlin kommt von Juso-Chef Philipp Türmer. Der Vorsitzende der SPD-Jugendorganisation sagte im ARD-Morgenmagazin, er sehe eine Chance in einem rot-grün-roten Bündnis. Vor allem die Krise auf dem Wohnungsmarkt könnte gemildert werden.
"Die Berlinerinnen und Berliner haben klargemacht, dass sie sich einen Politikwechsel wünschen", insbesondere bei den hohen Mieten, so Türmer. "Sie vertrauen diesem Bündnis, dass sie endlich etwas dagegen machen."
Ein Gesetz gegen Vergesellschaftung hält Türmer für unrealistisch. "Ich halte es für verfassungswidrig, den Ländern etwas zu verbieten, was die Verfassung ihnen garantiert."
Scharfe Kritik von CDU und CSU
Aus der Union kommt besonders scharfe Kritik an den Plänen für Vergesellschaftung. CSU-Chef Markus Söder sprach beim "Deutschlandtag" der Jungen Union von absurden Enteignungsfantasien von Sozialisten.
Unionsfraktionschef Thorsten Frei bezeichnete Vergesellschaftungen als das Dümmste, was man machen könne. Es werde Geld, das Berlin nicht habe, für Wohnungen ausgegeben, die es schon gebe. Zudem würden Investoren verschreckt, so Frei bei Caren Miosga.
Pläne für Verbot von Vergesellschaftungen
Die Bundesregierung hatte bereits im Juli beschlossen, dass sie eine solche Überführung in Gemeineigentum, die das Grundgesetz prinzipiell erlaubt, verhindern will. Vor allem die Union befürchtet durch die rot-grün-roten Pläne einen Schaden für den Wirtschaftsstandort Deutschland.
Bislang gibt es allerdings noch keinen Gesetzentwurf, sondern nur einen Beschluss des Koalitionsausschusses.
Bei einer Enteignung nach Artikel 14 des Grundgesetzes (GG) werden konkrete Eigentumsrechte für bestimmte Vorhaben, die dem "Wohle der Allgemeinheit" dienen, entzogen - etwa Grundstücke für eine Autobahn oder einen Deich. Wollen die Grundstückseigentümer nicht verkaufen, können sie in bestimmten Fällen enteignet werden. Dafür gibt es eingespielte rechtliche Verfahren mit Entschädigungszahlungen für die enteigneten Besitzer. Allein im Straßenbau gibt es jedes Jahr eine dreistellige Zahl an Enteignungsverfahren.
Bei einer Vergesellschaftung nach Artikel 15 GG geht es hingegen darum, "Grund und Boden, Naturschätze und Produktionsmittel" in Gemeineigentum zu überführen. Allerdings kam Artikel 15 noch nie zur Anwendung. Es geht damit um absolutes rechtliches Neuland. Auch hier müssten Art und Ausmaß der Entschädigung gesetzlich geregelt werden. Die Bezeichnung Enteignung ist in der politischen Debatte verständlich, juristisch aber unpräzise.
Mit Material der Nachrichtenagentur dpa und Informationen der ARD-Rechtsredaktion in Karlsruhe

title: Польща отримала балістичні ракети дальністю майже 300 км: на що здатна нова зброя
content_c:
Польща отримала балістичні ракети дальністю майже 300 км: на що здатна нова зброя
Польська армія отримала нову партію південнокорейських балістичних ракет CTM-290, здатних уражати цілі на відстані до 290 кілометрів. Варшава продовжує нарощувати ракетний арсенал і готується до власного виробництва боєприпасів.
Польща отримала нову партію балістичних ракет CTM-290 із дальністю ураження до 290 кілометрів. Боєприпаси призначені для реактивних систем залпового вогню Homar-K, які перебувають на озброєнні польської армії.
Про це повідомляє Мілітарний із посиланням на Агенцію озброєнь Польщі.
До нової партії увійшли два типи ракет: керовані реактивні снаряди CGR-080, здатні уражати цілі на відстані до 80 кілометрів, та балістичні ракети CTM-290 із дальністю до 290 кілометрів.
Водночас польське оборонне відомство не розкриває, скільки саме ракет отримали військові.
На що здатні нові балістичні ракети Польщі
Балістичні ракети CTM-290 призначені для використання з реактивних систем залпового вогню Homar-K. Це польська модифікація південнокорейського ракетного комплексу K239 Chunmoo.
Систему встановлюють на восьмиколісне шасі польського виробництва Jelcz та оснащують системою управління вогнем TOPAZ.
Пускова установка має два контейнери, кожен із яких може вміщувати шість керованих ракет CGR-080 або одну балістичну CTM-290.
Таким чином, одна установка Homar-K здатна нести до 12 керованих реактивних снарядів або дві балістичні ракети.
Перші успішні випробування CTM-290 відбулися у квітні 2024 року в Південній Кореї. За пусками спостерігали представники польського Міністерства оборони.
Польща нарощує ракетне озброєння
Постачання нових ракет відбувається в межах масштабної програми переозброєння польської ракетної артилерії.
Загалом Варшава планує закупити 290 пускових модулів Homar-K.
У квітні 2024 року Польща уклала додатковий контракт із південнокорейською компанією Hanwha Aerospace на постачання 72 пускових модулів та кількох тисяч ракет різної дальності.
Вартість цієї угоди становила близько 1,6 мільярда доларів.
Коли Польща почне виробляти власні ракети
Паралельно Варшава працює над локалізацією виробництва ракетних боєприпасів.
Польська компанія WB Electronics та південнокорейська Hanwha Aerospace домовилися про спільне виробництво керованих ракет калібру 239 мм.
За планами Агенції озброєнь, перші ракети польського виробництва мають зійти з конвеєра вже 2028 року.
Для цього в польському місті Гожув-Великопольський готують будівництво спеціалізованого підприємства.
Водночас початок постачань за окремим контрактом на ракети CGR-080 польського виробництва передбачений від 2030 року.
Розширення власного виробництва дозволить Польщі зменшити залежність від іноземних постачальників і забезпечити армію боєприпасами для далекобійних ракетних систем.
Нагадаємо, що тим часом британські військові готуються до можливої місії в Україні: що відпрацьовуватимуть у Польщі

title: Colorado wildlife overpass cut vehicle-animal collisions by 91%, report finds
content_c:
Colorado officials have tracked herds of elk, bears, pronghorn and even northern leopard frogs ambling across its new wildlife overpass. According to a newly released report, the overpass, which acts as a bridge over a busy stretch of interstate, has helped cut wildlife-vehicle collisions by 91% since its completion 10 months ago.
The overpass is the centerpiece of a larger system built by the state to assist wildlife crossing the highway, which also includes miles of 8-ft tall fencing and five large wildlife underpasses.
“One of the most heartwarming moments for me was when [Colorado department of transportation] sent me a picture of an elk mama taking her calf under [Interstate-25],” Brandon Marette, a wildlife biologist for Colorado parks and wildlife, told CBS News. “All came to fruition in that one moment. That elk with her calf was just standing there in safety.”
The Colorado department of transportation said before the overpass system was built, there was an average of one wildlife-vehicle crash a day in this corridor.
Such wildlife crossings are popping up across the country as a way to protect wildlife habitat and reduce collisions, which can result in injuries and deaths in humans and animals. Research has shown that overpass systems are successful in “nearly eliminating” these accidents and that such infrastructure buildouts often “pay for themselves” by preventing costly crashes.
Nearly 20 wildlife crossings are under way in the US, with the structure in Colorado currently the biggest. The overpass, which sits between the state’s two biggest cities, Denver and Colorado Springs, spans six lanes of traffic and connects 39,000 acres of habitat on both sides of the interstate. The bridge is covered in grass and measures 200ft wide and 209ft long with gradually sloped entrances to ease crossings for animals.
This region of Colorado is known for high movement of large game. State officials say that wildlife underpasses and tunnels often don’t work for big animals, such as bull elk, because they restrict mobility and don’t accommodate their antlers.
“Elk and pronghorn like these big open structures where they can see for miles in each direction,” Chuck Attardo, the environmental manager for Colorado department of transportation, told CBS News. “For decades, pronghorn going from Trinidad to Greenland were looking for a place to cross on I-25. And when we open this up, we have pronghorn on video using the overpass, and for the first time in decades they’re coming over here to the west side.”
While large game animals have been taking advantage of the crossing, officials have also tracked smaller wildlife using the corridor, including mule deer, coyotes, rabbits, frogs and the threatened Preble’s meadow jumping mouse.
The project received $22m in federal funding and $8m from the state, but officials say they were able to complete it for just $15m. Now, the Colorado department of transportation says it is hoping to build other wildlife crossings across the state.

title: Bulgarien: Angriff auf Starlink-Antennen – Haftbefehl gegen Deutsche erlassen
content_c:
Mutmaßliche Sabotage Brand an Starlink-Antennen in Bulgarien – Haftbefehl gegen Deutsche
Nach dem Brand an Starlink-Antennen in Bulgarien ist ein europäischer Haftbefehl gegen zwei Deutsche erlassen worden. Ein Gericht in Sofia gab einem entsprechenden Antrag der Staatsanwaltschaft statt, sagte eine Gerichtssprecherin der Nachrichtenagentur dpa. Zuvor hatten bulgarische Medien berichtet.
Die Tatverdächtigen im Alter von 19 Jahren sollen laut Anklage am 9. Oktober mehrere Antennen südlich von Sofia in Brand gesetzt haben. Laut einem Bericht des öffentlich-rechtlichen Rundfunks BNT geht es um 18 Anlagen, drei davon wurden übereinstimmenden Medienberichten zufolge komplett zerstört. Das prowestliche Oppositionsbündnis Demokratisches Bulgarien (DB), das den Vorfall öffentlich machte, hatte von elf angezündeten Antennen gesprochen.
Den Männern drohen Haftstrafen von drei bis zwölf Jahren. Ihre Verteidiger wollen Berufung einlegen.
Mutmaßliche Täter kamen über Serbien
Die beiden Verdächtigen waren laut Anklage als Touristen aus Serbien eingereist. Dorthin seien sie bereits nach wenigen Stunden zurückgekehrt – mit einem Auto mit deutschem Kennzeichen. Dieses ist laut BNT auf einen weiteren Deutschen zugelassen.
Der Leiter des bulgarischen Inlandsgeheimdiensts, Plamen Tontschew, geht mit Blick auf den Brand von Sabotage aus. »Derartige Sabotageakte sind auch in Zukunft nicht ausgeschlossen«, sagte er in einer Fragestunde des Parlaments.
In den vergangenen Wochen kam es vermehrt zu Angriffen auf Starlink-Infrastruktur. Ende September brannte eine Bodenstation südlich von Warschau, die polnische Regierung vermutet russische Geheimdienste hinter der Tat. Zwei Tatverdächtige wurden in Nürtingen bei Stuttgart festgenommen. Zuletzt machte Litauens Ministerpräsident Mindaugas Sinkevičius öffentlich, dass es auch am Rande von Vilnius einen versuchten Brandanschlag auf eine Starlink-Basisstation gegeben hatte.
Das Satellitennetz Starlink ist ein strategisch wichtiger Bestandteil der ukrainischen Verteidigung gegen Russlands Angriffskrieg.
description: Zwei 19-Jährige sollen in Bulgarien mehrere Starlink-Antennen angezündet haben. Laut Anklage kommen sie aus Deutschland und flüchteten mit einem deutschen Wagen. Ihnen drohen mehrere Jahre Haft.

Die beiden Verdächtigen waren laut Anklage als Touristen aus Serbien eingereist. Dorthin seien sie bereits nach wenigen Stunden zurückgekehrt – mit einem Auto mit deutschem Kennzeichen. Dieses ist laut BNT auf einen weiteren Deutschen zugelassen.
Der Leiter des bulgarischen Inlandsgeheimdiensts, Plamen Tontschew, geht mit Blick auf den Brand von Sabotage aus. »Derartige Sabotageakte sind auch in Zukunft nicht ausgeschlossen«, sagte er in einer Fragestunde des Parlaments.
In den vergangenen Wochen kam es vermehrt zu Angriffen auf Starlink-Infrastruktur. Ende September brannte eine Bodenstation südlich von Warschau, die polnische Regierung vermutet russische Geheimdienste hinter der Tat. Zwei Tatverdächtige wurden in Nürtingen bei Stuttgart festgenommen. Zuletzt machte Litauens Ministerpräsident Mindaugas Sinkevičius öffentlich, dass es auch am Rande von Vilnius einen versuchten Brandanschlag auf eine Starlink-Basisstation gegeben hatte.
Das Satellitennetz Starlink ist ein strategisch wichtiger Bestandteil der ukrainischen Verteidigung gegen Russlands Angriffskrieg.

title: Marktbericht: Neue Woche, neue Sorgen
content_c:
DAX verliert 1,2 Prozent Neue Woche, neue Sorgen
Die Börse gleicht derzeit einem Wechselbad. Die Gewinne von Freitag sind wieder dahin. Belastend wirkte neben den anhaltenden KI-Sorgen die Lage in Frankreich.
Zu Beginn der neuen Woche hat der DAX seine jüngsten Gewinne wieder eingebüßt. Der deutsche Leitindex schloss 1,2 Prozent tiefer bei 25.319 Punkten, nachdem er zeitweise schon 1,6 Prozent verloren hatte. Am Freitag hatte er noch die KI- und Inflationssorgen abgeschüttelt und ein Prozent auf 25.623 Zähler gewonnen.
In New York hatten die Technologiewerte am Freitagabend aber wegen der Sorge um die Nachhaltigkeit der KI-Rally erneut nachgegeben, was den Nasdaq 100 auf den tiefsten Stand seit vier Wochen zurückwarf. Heute ist die Technologiebörse deutlich erholt in den Tag gestartet, was auch den deutschen Markt etwas entlastete. Die Standardwerte des Dow Jones traten dagegen auf der Stelle.
Am Morgen meldete China ein unerwartet starkes Wirtschaftswachstum für das dritte Quartal. Das geht allerdings zum Teil auf Kosten anderer Volkswirtschaften: Ein Export-Boom von allein 36 Prozent im September legt nah, dass günstige chinesische Produkte europäische und deutsche Hersteller verdrängen.
Schwerer wogen aber die Sorgen um Frankreich. In der zweitgrößten Volkswirtschaft der EU bleibt die Frage, wie es nach der Gewalteskalation nach den Massenprotesten in vielen Regionen weitergeht. Französische Aktien und Anleihen standen nach Tagen relativer Ruhe wieder stark unter Druck. Die Rendite für zehnjährige Papiere liegt mit 4,9 Prozent wieder auf dem höchsten Stand seit dem Jahr 2002. Die Stimmung belastete auch den Euro.
Entspannung gab es am Ölmarkt. Die Nordseesorte Brent rückte von ihrem Fünf-Monats-Hoch vom Freitag wieder etwas ab. Allerdings kamen unterschiedliche Signale aus der Krisenregion um den Persischen Golf. Einerseits gab es erneut Angriffe auf zwei Tanker. Außerdem griff die Huthi-Miliz aus dem Jemen erneut Saudi-Arabien an.
US-Energieminister Chris Wright versuchte dagegen, die Gemüter zu beruhigen. Laut Wright haben sich die Öllieferungen aus dem Persischen Golf auf etwa 80 Prozent ihres Niveaus vor dem Konflikt erholt. Die Lieferungen von Raffinerieprodukten seien aber weiterhin eingeschränkt. Er stehe in Gesprächen mit europäischen Verbündeten, um Dieselvorräte freizugeben, sagte Wright.
Die Aktie der DHL Group verlor 0,9 Prozent. Am Freitag nach Börsenschluss hatte das Unternehmen prozentual zweistellige Zuwächsen bei Umsatz und Ergebnis im dritten Quartal gemeldet und seine Jahresprognose angehoben. Ein Händler wertete den neuen Ausblick positiv, eine komplette Überraschung sei er aber nicht. Zudem waren die Papiere zuletzt schon gut gelaufen.
Eine Großübernahme meldete dagegen Merck. Der Darmstädter Pharma- und Technologiekonzern übernimmt die britische Biotechfirma Silence Therapeutics. Mit der Transaktion, die rund 980 Millionen Euro kosten soll, will Merck sein Engagement im Bereich seltener Krankheiten stärken.
Die Aktie der Norma Group gab deutlich nach, nachdem der Autozulieferer seine Strategie bis 2031 vorgestellt hatte. Der Hersteller von Verbindungstechnik will mit seiner neuen Aufstellung leicht wachsen und dabei deutlich profitabler werden. Für etwas Verstimmung sorgte aber die Aussicht auf eine geringere Dividende. Ab 2027 sollen nämlich nur noch mindestens zehn Prozent des bereinigten Jahresergebnisses ausgeschüttet werden anstelle der bisher versprochenen 30 bis 35 Prozent.
In Berlin hat heute eine Investorenkonferenz begonnen, bei dem die Bundesregierung für den Standort werben will. Eingeladen sind Vertreterinnen und Vertreter zahlreicher Unternehmen aus Deutschland und dem Ausland, darunter der Chef des US-Chipherstellers Nvidia, Jensen Huang. Wie es aus Regierungskreisen hieß, plant die Bundesregierung eine Kooperation mit Nvidia.

title: Україна не може збивати реактивні "Шахеди" через обмеження Starlink: Флеш пояснив небезпеку
content_c:
Україна не може збивати реактивні "Шахеди" через обмеження Starlink: Флеш пояснив небезпеку
Обмеження роботи супутникового зв'язку Starlink заважають українським військовим використовувати дрони-перехоплювачі проти швидкісних російських безпілотників. Фахівець із радіотехнологій Сергій Бескрестнов закликав США зняти обмеження, які послаблюють українську протиповітряну оборону.
Україна зіткнулася із серйозними проблемами у протидії російським реактивним "Шахедам" через обмеження роботи супутникового зв'язку Starlink. Українські розробники створюють швидкісні дрони-перехоплювачі, однак через втрату зв'язку їхнє ефективне застосування ускладнене.
Про це розповів радник президента України з питань оборонних технологій Сергій Бескрестнов, відомий як Флеш, в інтерв'ю BBC.
Чому Україна не може ефективно перехоплювати реактивні "Шахеди"
За словами Бескрестнова, супутниковий зв'язок Starlink широко застосовується українськими військовими не лише для ударів по російських об'єктах, а й для захисту українських міст.
Особливо гостро проблема постала через використання Росією реактивних ударних безпілотників, які рухаються значно швидше за звичайні "Шахеди".
Для боротьби з ними українські фахівці розробляють спеціальні швидкісні перехоплювачі. Однак запроваджені обмеження роботи Starlink заважають підтримувати стабільний зв'язок із такими апаратами під час польоту.
«Це створює для нас проблему, оскільки ми не можемо захистити країну від реактивних "Шахедів". Це справді величезна проблема для нас», — наголосив Бескрестнов.
Він пояснив, що частина людей помилково вважає, нібито супутниковий зв'язок потрібен Україні переважно для далекобійних атак. Насправді від нього залежать і оборонні операції, зокрема робота дронів-перехоплювачів.
Флеш звернувся до США із закликом
За словами радника президента, Україна намагається пояснити американським партнерам, наскільки важливою є стабільна робота супутникового зв'язку для оборони держави.
Йдеться про компанію SpaceX, її засновника Ілона Маска, Пентагон та президента США Дональда Трампа.
Бескрестнов наголосив, що Starlink забезпечує не лише виконання бойових завдань, а й можливість українських військових підтримувати зв'язок зі своїми родинами.
Українська сторона закликає партнерів скасувати обмеження, які перешкоджають застосуванню швидкісних безпілотників для захисту від російських атак.
Що відомо про обмеження Starlink
Раніше стало відомо, що військові термінали супутникового зв'язку Starshield, створеного на основі Starlink, почали втрачати з'єднання під час руху на високих швидкостях.
За словами українських посадовців, на окремих ділянках фронту проблеми виникали за швидкості приблизно 130–161 км/год.
Такі обмеження вплинули не лише на використання ударних безпілотників, а й на фронтову логістику та роботу протиповітряної оборони.
Агентство Reuters із посиланням на американських і західних посадовців повідомляло, що рішення обмежити роботу Starshield для України надійшло з Білого дому. Водночас президент США Дональд Трамп та держсекретар Марко Рубіо заперечували причетність до запровадження обмежень.
Україна веде переговори зі SpaceX та американською стороною щодо зняття швидкісних обмежень, а також розглядає альтернативні системи супутникового зв'язку.
Нагадаємо, Ілон Маск заявив, що обмеження роботи Starshield для України є рішенням американської влади, а не SpaceX.

title: New AI tool can predict cancer survival by a single patient selfie, study suggests
content_c:
Doctors have developed an artificial intelligence tool that can predict a cancer patient’s chances of survival from a single photograph of their face.
The AI system was custom-built by experts at Mass General Brigham, a nonprofit, integrated academic healthcare system in Massachusetts, to estimate biological age and directly predict survival outcomes in patients diagnosed with cancer.
It is one of the most comprehensive demonstrations to date of how AI analysis of a selfie could help assess a patient’s health and potentially guide their medical care, and was trained on data from more than 40 million facial photographs across a range of ethnicities and ages.
Details of the breakthrough were published in the Lancet Digital Health journal.
The system can estimate a person’s biological age – the age a person looks, rather than their actual, chronological age – and predict the chances of survival for cancer patients from an ordinary photograph of their face, according to the results of a study that examined the model.
Doctors used the technology to develop two complementary tools. FAHR-FaceAge estimates a patient’s biological age, and predicts cancer survival. FAHR-FaceSurvival predicts survival from a facial photograph directly, rather than inferring survival through biological age.
Although FAHR-FaceAge and FAHR-FaceSurvival were derived from the same model, they captured different and complementary information about a patient’s health.
Each algorithm also relied on distinct parts of the face to make respective predictions of age and mortality risk. FAHR-FaceAge focuses on the creases that run from the sides of the nose down to the corners of the mouth, the forehead area just above the eye sockets, and the temples. FAHR-FaceSurvival, meanwhile, evaluates the region below the eyes and around the nasal bridge.
“FAHR-FaceSurvival advances the field of facial health recognition AI a step further by learning survival risk directly from facial photographs of patients with cancer,” said Hugo Aerts, a co-senior author of the study. “To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration that an AI model can directly predict cancer survival from a simple photograph.”
Among cancer patients treated with radiotherapy in the US, the people who, according to FAHR-FaceAge, looked five or more years older than their actual age had a 21% higher risk of dying during the average four-year follow-up than the rest of the group. The patients who looked five or more years younger had a 17% lower risk.
“The key technical advance is that FAHR-Face learns a general representation of the face from more than 40 million images, which can then be adapted to distinct health outcomes such as biological age and survival,” said Aerts. “This foundation-model approach gives us a scalable way to develop multiple facial health biomarkers rather than training each model from scratch.”
The results of the study suggest people’s biological age estimates are closely linked to their physical health, which could reflect their ability to survive certain treatments.
The breakthrough could pave the way for AI facial analysis to assist doctors in making difficult decisions about the best way forward in terms of treatment for their patients.
The tool could help better predict the risk of death or complications after major surgery or other treatments for cancer.
Dr Raymond Mak, a radiation oncologist at Mass General Brigham, said: “As the population ages, physicians need better ways to estimate physical reserve and frailty before recommending intensive treatments such as radiation, surgery or systemic therapy.
“Our goal is to make face photograph-based health assessment more quantitative, consistent and scalable so it can support personalised treatment decisions rather than replace physician judgment.”
Researchers found lifestyle factors were associated with facial ageing. For example, heavy alcohol use, drug use and smoking were linked to looking biologically older in AI analysis of facial photographs.
“Another surprising finding was how consistent FAHR-FaceAge was across common real-world photo variations, including pose, lighting, facial expression and makeup,” said Mak. “It was also stable across most tested plastic surgery procedures, with only a small shift observed after rhinoplasty.”
Doctors cautioned that while single facial photographs could offer an easy, low-cost way to support personalised treatment decisions, more research was needed before the tool could be widely used.
